questions.question: What does `await` actually do?
options: Runs the awaited code on a new thread in parallel
Pauses the current async method until the awaited operation completes, without blocking the thread
Immediately returns a default value and skips the operation
Converts synchronous code into a Task automatically
questions.explanation: await suspends the current method at that point until the Task completes, but frees up the thread to do other work in the meantime — that's the whole point, unlike Thread.Sleep or .Result which block.

questions.question: What should the return type of an async method that produces a `string` be?
options: `string`
`Task<string>`
`async string`
`void`
questions.explanation: Async methods that produce a value return `Task<T>` — the T being the eventual result type. Callers `await` it to get the actual `string` out.

questions.question: What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing, this is a normal way to call async code
`.Result` blocks the thread synchronously waiting for the Task, defeating the purpose of async and risking deadlocks — use `await` instead
It doesn't compile
DownloadReportAsync must be called with parentheses only, never with .Result
questions.explanation: `.Result` (and `.Wait()`) force the calling thread to block until the Task finishes — exactly the freezing behavior async/await exists to avoid. Always `await` instead.

questions.question: What's the benefit of `await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3)` over `await t1; await t2; await t3;` (three separate awaits)?
options: No benefit, they're identical
WhenAll lets all three run CONCURRENTLY and waits for all to finish together, rather than waiting for each one fully before starting the next
WhenAll is required syntax, the other form doesn't compile
WhenAll only works with two tasks, never three
questions.explanation: Awaiting each Task individually in sequence means t2 doesn't even START until t1 fully finishes. If t1/t2/t3 are independent (e.g. three unrelated downloads), starting them all first and then WhenAll-ing is much faster.

questions.question: In async code, why avoid `Thread.Sleep` in favor of `await Task.Delay(...)`?
options: Thread.Sleep is deprecated and won't compile
Thread.Sleep blocks the entire thread, reintroducing the exact freezing problem async/await is meant to solve; Task.Delay frees the thread while waiting
They behave identically
Task.Delay is always faster
questions.explanation: Thread.Sleep blocks synchronously — nothing else can run on that thread while it sleeps. Task.Delay, when awaited, releases the thread to do other work until the delay elapses.

questions.question: try/catch around an `await` call works exactly the same as around any normal synchronous call.
questions.explanation: Exceptions thrown inside an awaited async operation surface at the await point and can be caught with an ordinary try/catch — no special async exception-handling syntax is needed.
